name: Vörösmarty Square
description: Vörösmarty Square is a central Pest square at the northern end of Váci Street, with a statue of the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, the Café Gerbeaud and the southern terminus of the M1 metro. It has carried many names since 1812 before taking the poet's in 1926.

children.text: Vörösmarty Square is a public square in central Pest at the northern end of Váci Street. At its centre stands the statue of the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, facing west, made by Eduard Telcs and Ede Kallós. Behind it is a fenced park and a fountain flanked by stone lions. Stairs at the north end lead down to the southern terminus of the M1 line of the Budapest Metro.

The square has had many names. In 1812 it was known as Theatro piatcza, after a theatre that stood on the site; in the 1830s it was Harmincad tér, then Játékszín tér, Séta tér in the 1840s, and German Theatre Square in 1846. It was Színház tér in 1850 and Old Theatre Square in 1866. In 1874 it became Gizella tér, after Archduchess Gisela of Austria; it was named Károlyi Mihály tér from 1918 to 1920, was Gizella tér again, and took its present name in 1926. A column in the square lists all its former names.

The square's metro station opened on 2 May 1896 as part of the first section of the Millennium Underground Railway, the first metro system in continental Europe. It was formerly called Gizella tér and was rebuilt in 1970. It is included in the UNESCO World Heritage Site listing for Budapest and Andrássy Avenue, which dates from 2002.

At the northern end of the square is Café Gerbeaud. According to Wikipedia, Henrik Kugler founded his confectionery in 1858 and moved it to this square, then called Gizella tér, in 1870, on the ground floor of the Pest Hungarian Commercial Bank. Emil Gerbeaud, born in Geneva, joined him as an associate in 1884 and gradually took over while keeping the original name. The shop was nationalised in 1948 and renamed Vörösmarty, regained its historical name in March 1984, and was extensively renovated after 1995.
Good to know
The M1 metro terminates under the square, so it is an easy meeting point on the Millennium line.
Váci Street, the pedestrian shopping street, starts here and runs south from the square.
Check the Café Gerbeaud website for current opening times and any seasonal events in the square.

historyIntro: Vörösmarty Square combines a busy modern shopping area with the memory of Hungarian literary life in the centre of Pest.

historySections.heading: A square shaped by culture and commerce

children.text: The square takes its present name from the nineteenth-century Hungarian poet Mihály Vörösmarty. The prominent monument to him anchors a public space surrounded by shops, cafés and significant city-centre façades.

historySections.heading: A meeting place through the seasons

children.text: The long association with cafés and street life continues in cultural events and winter markets. The square's changing uses show how a city centre can carry national literary memory while functioning as an everyday meeting place.

name: The 1956 Monument
description: The 1956 Monument, put up in 2006 on the fiftieth anniversary of the uprising, is a government-commissioned memorial made of rusting steel columns that converge in a wedge. It stands on ground where a Stalin statue was pulled down in 1956, and it has stirred debate in Hungary ever since.

children.text: The 1956 Monument is a memorial to the 1956 Hungarian uprising, in Városliget, the City Park. It was dedicated in 2006, on the fiftieth anniversary of the revolution, and was commissioned by the Hungarian government. The design is by the i-ypszilon art group, which includes Tamás Emdi-Kiss, Katalin György, Csaba Horváth and Tamás Papp.

The site has its own history. The memorial stands where a large statue of Stalin was toppled by freedom fighters in 1956, leaving only its boots on the plinth. The monument itself is made of rusting steel columns. According to one description, they represent people gathering in growing numbers and merging into one strong force that breaks through the road in front of it.

The monument has not been uncontroversial. One source says it has drawn criticism on artistic grounds, and some see it as a government effort to rewrite history and claim credit that belongs to others. A 2006 Daily Telegraph report quoted by the same source says that opponents wanted a traditional heroic sculpture depicting people, and some critics read the steel posts as gallows, recalling the hangings after the revolution. The war-memorial.net database also notes that it created a heated debate in Hungary at the time.

For a visitor, it is worth reading the monument as a public argument as much as a piece of sculpture: its form, its location on a Stalin-statue site and the way people respond to it all reflect how Hungary remembers 1956.
Good to know
It is in City Park (Városliget), so it combines with other City Park sights in the same visit.
Look at the way the steel columns converge, and consider the different readings of the form described above.
Read about the 1956 uprising before you go; the monument says more once you know the events it commemorates.

heroImage.creditTitle: Budapest, City Park, Denkmal der Revolution 2015-08 (3).jpg

historyIntro: The 1956 Monument remembers the Hungarian Revolution through a deliberately modern sculptural language of resistance and shared purpose.

children.text: The monument near City Park commemorates the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence. The work by the i-Ypszilon group was inaugurated on 23 October 2006, fifty years after the revolution began.

Many vertical steel columns, in rusted and stainless steel, rise in an increasingly dense wedge. One description reads them as people gathering in growing numbers and merging into one strong force, while the 56-degree angle of the wedge alludes to 1956.
The memorial is described as a wedge at a 56-degree angle, and a tourism source says its axis makes that angle with Dózsa György Road. The number alludes to the year of the revolution.

name: Gresham Palace
description: Gresham Palace is an Art Nouveau office and apartment building at the Pest end of the Chain Bridge, built in 1904-1906 for a London insurer. After decades of decline it was restored and reopened as a hotel in 2004, with Zsolnay ceramics, mosaics and peacock ironwork among its details.

children.text: Gresham Palace stands on the Danube bank beside Széchenyi Square and the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. It was built as the Budapest headquarters of the London-based Gresham Life Assurance Company, which took its name from Sir Thomas Gresham, the sixteenth-century English financier who founded the Royal Exchange. The company bought the site in 1880, where the neoclassical Nákó House of 1827 had stood. The new building was designed by the local architects Zsigmond Quittner and József Vágó, and one source also names László Vágó.

Construction began in 1904, the building was completed in 1906 and it opened in 1907. It combined shops and a café on the ground floor, company offices above and apartments for senior staff and others on the upper floors. It is a prominent example of Art Nouveau in Hungary. According to We Love Budapest, Géza Maróti made the facade reliefs, Miksa Róth the glass and mosaics, the Zsolnay factory supplied ceramics, and Gyula Jungfer made the wrought ironwork, which includes peacock motifs. The only surviving original stained-glass window, on the first-floor stairwell, depicts Lajos Kossuth.

The twentieth century was unkind to the building. In the Second World War the Red Army used it as barracks, and afterwards the shops and flats were nationalised and it lost its former prestige. It became decrepit and was used as an apartment building under the People's Republic. In 1990 the national government gave the palace to the city of Budapest, and over the following decade several hotel plans came and went because of legal disputes and changes of ownership.

Restoration finally followed a 2001 purchase, with the large staircase, stained glass, mosaics, ironwork and winter gardens brought back, and the hotel reopened in June 2004. It is now the Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace, with 179 guest rooms, including 17 suites, and the State General Reserve Fund of Oman bought it in 2011. Even if you are not a guest, the facade and the ironwork with its peacock motifs can be admired from the street, and the building sits beside the bridge approach and Széchenyi Square.
Good to know
Look up at the facade reliefs, and at the wrought ironwork with its peacock motifs, from the pavement.
The palace faces the Chain Bridge, so it pairs naturally with a bridge crossing and a walk to Adam Clark Square.
It is a hotel now; check the hotel's website for what areas and services are open to non-guests.

heroImage.alt: The Art Nouveau facade of Gresham Palace beside the Chain Bridge

historyIntro: Gresham Palace is a celebrated example of Budapest Art Nouveau, built for a commercial city and later transformed into a luxury hotel.

historySections.heading: A prestigious building at the Chain Bridge

children.text: The palace was developed on Széchenyi István Square during the early twentieth century. Its flowing ornament, wrought metalwork and decorated interior reflect the artistic ambitions of the Art Nouveau period.

Over time the building's uses changed, and extensive restoration helped revive its architectural details. The landmark now houses a hotel, while its exterior continues to define the view towards Chain Bridge.

name: Hungarian Academy of Sciences
description: The Hungarian Academy of Sciences, founded in 1825 after Count István Széchenyi offered a year's income from his estates, has its seat in a Neo-Renaissance palace on the Pest bank. Designed by the Berlin architect Friedrich August Stüler and inaugurated in 1865, it is decorated with statues of scholars.

children.text: The Hungarian Academy of Sciences has its seat in a palace on the Pest bank of the Danube, between Széchenyi rakpart and Akadémia utca, facing what is today Roosevelt Square. The Academy was founded in 1825: at a debate of the Diet in Pressburg (now Bratislava) on 3 November 1825, Count István Széchenyi offered a year's income from his estates, and other delegates followed his example. Its task was to develop the Hungarian language and to study and promote the sciences and arts in Hungarian. It received its current name in 1845.

The palace was designed by Friedrich August Stüler, the Prussian king's architect, who produced the main facade and floor plan and chose many of the architectural and sculptural ornaments. The facade inscriptions give 1860 for the start and 1864 for the completion, and the building was inaugurated in 1865. The Academy describes it as an early, mature example of Hungarian neo-Renaissance architecture, blending Northern Italian Renaissance with Berlin neo-Renaissance tendencies. Its construction sparked heated debate, partly because the style could not grow from local tradition after the events of 1848.

Terracotta statues of scholars and allegorical figures were ordered from Berlin, with moulds by the sculptor Emil Wolff; the exception is the statue of Miklós Révai, made by Miklós Izsó, who also made the coat of arms above the central window. The main facade has statues of Galileo and Révai, the Danube facade Newton and Lomonosov, and the Akadémia Street facade Descartes and Leibniz. Lomonosov replaced Raphael after the Second World War.

Inside, the ceremonial hall has a coved vault whose ornamental elements were designed by Albert Schickedanz, with triptychs by Károly Lotz on its east and west walls showing St Stephen and King Matthias. In the vestibule, a marble relief by Barnabás Holló, installed in 1914 to commemorate Queen Elizabeth, glorifies the Compromise of 1867. The Second World War badly damaged the Scientists' Club rooms in the Akadémia Street wing, which were rebuilt in the 1950s. For many visitors the palace is simply a landmark on the riverside, a building that represents the nineteenth-century effort to make science and scholarship Hungarian.
Good to know
The palace is best enjoyed from outside: walk around it to find the statues on the Danube, Akadémia Street and square facades.
Check the Academy's official site for current opening times and whether any exhibition or hall is open to visitors.
The palace faces the Danube on the Pest bank; it is a good stop on a riverside walk.

heroImage.alt: The neo-Renaissance building of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences on the Pest embankment

historyIntro: The Academy's Danube-facing palace is a monument to Hungarian scholarly life and to the cultural confidence of nineteenth-century Budapest.

historySections.heading: Science takes a place on the riverfront

children.text: The Academy's monumental headquarters was completed in 1865. The design by Friedrich August Stüler takes inspiration from Renaissance palaces, bringing a distinctive formality to the Danube embankment.

The institution has long stood for Hungarian learning and public debate. Its façade is also part of the famous riverside urban landscape, linking scientific heritage with the development of Pest as a capital.
